Journal of Financial Economics 30 (1991) 3-43. North-Holland

Union negotiations and corporate policy

A study of labor concessions in the domestic steel industry during the 1980s”

Ha.rry DeAngelo and Linda DeAngelo

University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA 90089, USA

Received March 1991, final version received November 1991

This paper studies managerial compensation, financial reporting, and dividend policies of the seven major domestic steel producers during requests for union concessions. Substantial layoffs, reported losses, and sacrifices by nonunion stakeholders buttressed managers’ case for union concessions. From 1980 to 1988, sample firms reduced their work force by about 300,000 (almost two-thirds) and annual wage payments from $16.1 to $8.6 billion. Reported income is lower during union negotiations, controlling for cash flows, as is managerial pay, with average CEO salary plus bonus declining 18%. Dividend reductions and white-collar pay cuts are substantial, pervasive, and clustered during union negotiations.

1. Introduction

Most studies of corporate policy focus on changes in one decision - in dividend payments, managerial compensation, or accounting choice - as de- termined by corporate performance. Largely unaddressed is the extent to which these decisions interact to reflect a consistent overall corporate strat- egy. For example, are changes in dividend policy linked to changes in managerial compensation? If so, do these corporate policy decisions reflect

strategic considerations, for example, information costs characteristic of the firm’s political environment, in addition to technological factors? Investiga- tion of these issues is difficult in large samples, since it requires analysis of a great deal of firm- and industry-specific data. Hence we focus on firms in one industry, the domestic integrated steel producers. These firms’ generous labor practices, established in prior negotiations with a powerful union, came under strong pressure in the 1980s as a result of changes in the competitive environment that also created incentives for managers to adjust corporate policy.

During the 1980s U.S. steel producers faced increased competition from subsidized imports and nonunionized mini-mills, the technological obsoles- cence of aging plants, and a decline in steel demand due to a worldwide recession. The resultant overcapacity led to years of massive losses - $3.2 billion in 1982, the first industry loss since the Great Depression, followed by $9.5 billion in the 1983-1986 period for the seven major integrated produc- ers.’ In 1982, domestic steel production fell to its lowest level since 1946, with capacity utilization at 48.1% for the major producers. (Steel production entails large fixed costs, with breakeven then estimated at 80-85% of capacity, in part because of high labor costs.) By 1982, the average domestic steelworker’s total wages and benefits exceeded by more than 60% those paid the more productive Japanese. Moreover, this competitive disadvantage was itself costly to remove, since existing labor agreements with the United Steelworkers of America (USW) granted severance benefits estimated as high as $60,000-$70,000 per steelworker.

Managers of domestic steel producers faced the difficult task of negotiating concessionary union agreements that would permit their firms to reduce capacity and modernize production in response to increased competition and declining demand. This paper studies adjustments in managerial compensa- tion, financial reporting, and dividend policy made by managers of the seven largest domestic steel producers during the period in which they negotiated substantial givebacks by unionized labor. These difficult labor negotiations led to the breakup of the multi-employer bargaining group that had bar- gained for the domestic steel industry for 30 years, and resulted in temporary wage reductions and other union concessions in both 1983 and 1986-1987.

The 1980s restructuring of the domestic steel industry had truly dramatic consequences for steel producers’ labor costs, employment, and productive capacity. The aggregate wage bill for the seven major producers, which totalled about $16.1 billion in 1980, declined a striking 46.6% to around $8.6

‘These firms, which make up our sample, had approximately two-thirds of the domestic steel industry’s productive capacity during the 1980s. The firms are U.S. Steel Corporation (now USX), LTV Corporation, Bethlehem Steel Corporation, Armco Inc., National Steel Corporation (later National Intergroup), Republic Steel Corporation (now owned by LTV), and Inland Steel Company.

Page 3

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 5

billion in 1988. This substantial reduction in total labor costs was largely achieved through radical employment cuts. Steelworker layoffs at the seven firms were pervasive and resulted in a net reduction of almost two-thirds of the work force, for a total loss of approximately 300,000 jobs over the decade. This radical employment decline reflects sample firms’ decisions to downsize operations that reduced their productive capacity by 38.2% from 1980 to 1988. To obtain labor concessions, managers must make a credible case that current economic conditions pose a serious threat to the firm’s competitive viability. Perhaps the most convincing evidence is that managers actually shut down some operations and effected large-scale layoffs. Substantial losses provide corroboratory evidence. We find that sample firms’ reported net income is significantly lower during union negotiations, controlling for cash flows, than in nonnegotiation years. The losses reported in negotiation years are largely driven by one-time special charges that reflect managers’ real restructuring decisions, but whose timing is discretionary across negotiation and nonnegotiation years. These charges are commonly taken late in the fourth quarter, when managers announce that they expect to shut down operations (or not reopen previously idled plants), announcements that could readily be deferred into the next fiscal year. It thus appears that managers of domestic steel firms deliberately reported larger losses during union negotia- tions to help their case for wage and other concessions from the USW.

We also find a consistent pattern in other managerial decisions that strengthens the case that serious financial problems require major conces- sions from unionized labor. Specifically, managers’ requests for union conces- sions were bolstered by substantial contemporaneous sacrifices by stakehold- ers other than union workers. We find pervasive pay cuts for white-collar workers, the timing of which seems designed to convince unionized labor to follow suit. Dividend reductions are also pervasive and are concentrated during union negotiations. Dividends were eliminated by six firms (although the median firm had paid dividends for 46 continuous years) and cut substantially by the seventh. Cash conserved via dividend reductions aggre- gates to several hundred million dollars per year which, while surely not trivial, is well below the billions of dollars in annual savings accomplished via layoffs and wage reductions.

Top management’s compensation was cut at all seven firms, with especially large reductions in union negotiation years, controlling for corporate perfor- mance. Chief executive officers (CEOs) experienced an average 18.1% de- cline in salary plus bonus in negotiation years (versus an average 19.5% increase in other years). For the five highest paid officers, salary plus bonus fell by an average 15.4% in union negotiation years (versus an average 16.0% increase in other years). Although these datk ‘ndicate that top managers took large percentage pay cuts during union negotiations, the resulting cash flow

Page 4

6 H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngeio, Restructuring of the steel industr)

savings are quite small compared to the annual labor cost savings we document. Top management’s financial sacrifices thus appear to be symbolic actions which indicate that they too will bear personally significant costs during the firm’s financial difficulties. In fact, top management often stresses its own sacrifices when attempting to gain concessions from unionized labor and other stakeholders.

Overall, our results conform closely to the political view of the corporate contracting process outlined in DeAngelo and DeAngelo (1990) on dividend policy and in Jensen and Murphy (1990a, b) on managerial compensation. DeAngelo and DeAngelo suggest that dividend reductions reflect managers’ desire to reconcile the interests of various claimants during periods of financial distress. Jensen and Murphy suggest that it is difficult to reward top management adequately for excellent performance because such rewards would engender significant protests from workers. The result is a contracting environment in which the payoffs to top management, unionized labor, and others are implicitly linked. Thus, when seeking union concessions, managers have incentives to induce and publicize sacrifices by all stakeholders, so that corporate policies are determined by strategic contracting considerations as well as by fundamental factors such as the firm’s technological capabilities, product market pressures, etc.

Section 2 of the paper briefly describes the competitive environment in the steel industry during the 1980s. Section 3 documents sample firms’ reductions in employment and labor costs, and describes the timing of union negotia- tions. Section 4 reports sample firms’ earnings and cash flow performance, and relates earnings performance and the timing of noncash writeoffs to the occurrence of union negotiations. Section 5 describes wage reductions for managerial and salaried personnel, and relates their timing to that of union negotiations. Section 6 relates the timing and stock price impact of dividend reductions to union negotiations. Section 7 concludes with a brief summary.

2. The domestic steel industry in the early 1980~~

In the early 1980s the U.S. steel industry consisted of seven major integrated producers that accounted for about two-thirds of domestic capac- ity, some smaller producers, and a number of domestic nonunionized mini- mills that reproduce steel from scrap. Steel is a primary input in the production of automobiles, industrial machinery and equipment for the construction, railroad, and shipbuilding industries, motors of all kinds, build-

‘This section’s discussion of overall conditions in the domestic steel industry is based on various issues of Standard & Poor’s Industry Surueys, articles in the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), and Hoerr (1988). The data in this and the following sections are compiled from corporate annual reports, forms lOK, proxy statements, the Center for Research in Security Prices and Compustat tapes, Moody’s Manuals, the American Iron and Steel Institute 1988 Annual Statistical Report, Standard & Poor’s Industry Surueys, and the WSJ.

Page 5

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 7

ings and bridges, office furniture, and appliances. Since most steel output is used in the production of capital goods, demand is highly cyclical. However, the costs of steel production - primarily production equipment and union- ized labor - are relatively fixed. Thus steel production is unprofitable at relatively low levels of output. At the beginning of the decade, the breakeven point for steel production was estimated at 80-85% of productive capacity (see, for example, Standard & Poor’s Industry Surveys, April 28, 1983. p. S15).

Before the worldwide recession of the early 198Os, a number of factors had already reduced the demand for domestic steel. First, the oil crisis of the early 1970s had encouraged automobile manufacturers to switch production toward lighter, more fuel-efficient cars that used more aluminum and plastic materials. (Automobile manufacturers, which accounted for 21.4% of do- mestic steel shipments in 1973, accounted for only 14.9% by 1980.) Second, imported steel had captured an increasing portion of domestic consumption - rising from 14.1% in 1976 to an eventual high of 26.2% in 1984 (Standard & Poor’s Industry Surveys, February 3, 1986, p. S26). Because of the importance of steel production to basic industry, many foreign govern- ments subsidized it, and the rising value of the dollar also helped foreign producers. Finally, integrated producers faced increased competition from domestic mini-mills that were able to reproduce steel from scrap at a cost advantage over new steel, both because of low prices for scrap and because they employed nonunionized labor. Substantial costs of exiting steel production exacerbated the resultant overcapacity problem. These costs were due primarily to existing labor agreements with the USW, and included severance pay, pension and health care benefits, unemployment insurance, and other supplemental unemploy- ment benefits. (They also included federally mandated environmental recla- mation costs.) The total employment costs of permanently closing a steel production facility were estimated to be as high as $60,000-$70,000 per employee (see, for example, ‘Bethlehem’s Plan to Slash Capacity Shows How Fast U.S. Steel Industry Is Shrinking’, The Wall Street Journal, December 29. 1982). The problem, as Fruhan (1985, p. 133) has pointed out, is that ‘if a steel company wants to close a plant, it becomes obligated to pay unreserved and unfunded pension and health care costs that generally far exceed the liquidation value of the plant and related working capital’.

Managers of domestic steel firms thus found themselves in a difficult dilemma - although capacity reductions were costly, so was maintaining production at current labor costs. By 1982, the average U.S. steelworker’s total wages and benefits had reached nearly $24 per hour. This figure exceeds by more than 60% what Japanese steelworkers earned, although the Japanese were estimated to be twice as productive (see, for example, Standard & Poor’s Industry Surveys, April 28, 1983, p. S15). It is also high relative to the

3. The timing and impact of labor concessions

Although the 1980 contract with the USW did not expire until August 1983, negotiations were opened early (in June 1982) to accommodate the steel industry’s request to bargain for wage concessions. For these talks, the seven major producers chose not to invoke the no-strike provisions of the ENA (because they were unwilling to grant the automatic wage increases it required). They held on-again, off-again negotiations with the union during

Page 9

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 11

1982, failing to reach an agreement first in July and again in November. Ultimately they reached a three and one-half year agreement that went into effect in March 1983. This agreement provided for a 9% reduction in hourly pay, and reductions in vacation pay, cost-of-living adjustments, and other benefits (with gradual reinstatement over the life of the contract) that were estimated to reduce 1983 aggregate labor costs by some $1.5 to $2 billion.

Dissent over how to negotiate the requisite union concessions caused the steel industry bargaining group to collapse before the expiration of the 1983 contract. As a result, the major steel firms negotiated separate labor agree- ments during 1986-1987 (for the first time in 30 years). LTV, Bethlehem Steel, National Intergroup, and Inland Steel had all negotiated wage agree- ments by the contract expiration date of July 31, 1986. LTV filed for bankruptcy in July, however, and soon thereafter began an attempt to negotiate a new contract (ratified in August 1987). Armco negotiated a three-month extension, and had reached an agreement with the USW by November 1986. U.S. Steel was struck by the USW on August 1, 1986; when a new contract was ratified in February 1987, the strike had lasted longer than any other in the industry’s history. Overall, 1986-1987 wage agreements provided for temporary wage and benefit concessions in return for an increase in profit sharing and job security.

Appendix A provides a more detailed chronology of union negotiations in the steel industry between 1980 and 1988. It indicates that industry requests for wage concessions were made during two periods: June 1982 to March

1983 for all firms, and January 1986 to August 1987, with exact dates differing for individual firms. In sections that follow, we relate changes in reported earnings and in managerial compensation to the presence or absence of union negotiations. All seven firms reported earnings on a calendar year basis (until National Steel switched to a March 31 year-end in 1986).

Accordingly, earnings released during requests for labor concessions are 1982 earnings for all seven firms, 1985 earnings for five firms (Republic had merged with LTV, reducing the sample to six firms, and U.S. Steel did not open talks until June 19861, and 1986 earnings for two firms (LTV and U.S. Steel had not settled by the 1986 earnings release date). Managerial compen- sation figures are taken to be those related to the same calendar years. For ease of discussion, we shall refer to these observations for 1982, 1985, and 1986 as ‘union negotiation years’. (Strictly speaking, these observations refer to financial data for 1982, 1985, and 1986 that are relevant for union negotiations held respectively in 1982-1983 and in 1986-1987.)

As a result of reductions in the work force, wage concessions, and productivity improvements, the seven major domestic steel producers experienced a sharp decline in total annual labor costs from 1980 to 1988. (Because sample firms do not systematically report wage expense and employment data for union versus nonunion employees or steel versus nonsteel employees, our

Alternatively, we can estimate the decline in steel-related labor costs by taking 1988 total labor costs times the ratio of steel revenue to total revenue in that year, minus the same calculation for 1980. Although our estimates necessarily include some imprecision (see footnote 7) and do not precisely separate steel-related union wages from other labor costs, their size leaves little doubt that (i) potential cost savings from renegotiating labor contracts were material at the beginning of the decade, and (ii> sample firms did, in fact, achieve material labor cost savings over the decade.

discussed earlier, contributed to the financial difficulties steel firms faced in the 1980s. As of 1980, steelworkers’ average hourly compensation repre- sented a 61% premium over the compensation of manufacturing workers (up from 24% in 1964 and, even more dramatically, from 16% as recently as 1970). After the union negotiations of the early to mid-1980s steelworkers’ hourly compensation premium shrank substantially, and leveled out to the 45-46% range by 1986-1988. Had steel firms paid in 1988 the 61% compensation premium they paid in 1980, the average steelworker would have received 10.3% greater compensa- tion. Accordingly, sample firms’ 1988 total wage bill of $8.6 billion would have been $9.5 billion, or almost $1 billion higher had steelworkers’ premium not been reduced from its 1980 level. (This estimate assumes that the level of employment is not reduced from its actual 1988 level in response to the hypothetical higher wage rate.) Had sample firms maintained employment at the 1980 level, their 1988 aggregate wage bill would have been higher by many billions of dollars, since they laid off almost two-thirds of their workforce over the period. Thus, while the cost savings from layoffs and dampened wage payments were each substantial in total dollar terms, layoffs were responsible for the bulk of the annual labor cost savings achieved by sample firms.

Appendix B provides a detailed description of the pervasive, large-scale steelworker layoffs and plant closures at sample firms during the 1980-1988 period. It indicates, for example, that Bethlehem Steel announced plans in 1982 to permanently shrink its steelmaking capacity by 20%, and to eliminate 10,000 jobs. Republic Steel announced layoffs in the same year that totaled 14,000 workers (more than one-third of its work force) and plans to shut down operations at several plants. In 1984, Inland announced further layoffs (beyond the 24% of its work force already laid off), and in 1985 announced plans to shut down operations representing 30% of productive capacity. The appendix documents numerous layoff announcements by each of these com- panies and for the remaining four sample firms.

Although layoffs and plant closings were announced throughout the early to mid-1980s the union negotiation year of 1982 saw especially large employ- ment reductions by sample firms. For all seven firms, appendix B indicates that more employees were let go in 1982 than in any other year between 1980 and 1988. It seems reasonable to believe that the large employment reduc- tions in 1982 primarily reflect the intense economic pressure to reduce capacity that sample firms were under at the time. But it is also clear that managers used threatened and actual layoffs and plant closings to back up their claims that labor concessions were essential. For example, after U.S. Steel failed in 1983 to obtain additional union concessions at selected plants, the firm announced it would close almost all of the marginal operations in question, reduce steel capacity by 17%, and eliminate 15,400 jobs (see the

Page 13

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 15

appendix A entry for December 1983 and the appendix B entry for U.S. Steel in 1983).

The threat of massive layoffs is a credible means of obtaining union concessions because the entire steel industry exhibited visible evidence of financial difficulty at the time. Should the USW fail to respond with wage concessions, their members stand to lose not only the value of any firm-specific human capital, but also the value of any industry-specific capital. This fact creates an incentive for managers of domestic steel producers to ‘pull together’ and jointly paint a picture of extreme financial distress to the union. Of course, managers of individual firms have incentives to create an even bleaker picture if they can thereby negotiate differential givebacks that provide an advantage over competitors - witness the bankruptcy filings of LTV and Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel and the latter firm’s 1981 expulsion from the multi-employer bargaining group.

4. Financial reporting strategy

One means managers can use to paint a bleak financial picture is to deliberately understate reported earnings. Although union leaders may be more financially sophisticated than the rank-and-file (and therefore better able to ‘see through’ managers’ accounting choices), they may themselves truly believe the firm’s condition merits concessions. Hence, low reported earnings may help union leaders convince the rank-and-file to accept contract terms that workers would ordinarily view as onerous. In any case, an empirical finding that earnings are more negative during union negotiations than would be predicted by sample firms’ contemporaneous cash flows would provide evidence that managers used their firm’s financial reporting strategy to encourage labor givebacks.”

Liberty and Zimmerman (1986) find no evidence of income-decreasing accounting choices by managers of firms in routine labor negotiations. Our finding of a significant relation is perhaps attributable to our focus on firms attempting to negotiate labor concessions, for which there is considerable other evidence of financial difficulty (for example, large-scale layoffs, man- agerial pay cuts, and dividend reductions). Relative to routine negotiations, requests for givebacks during visible signs of financial difficulty enable man- agers to depress income with fewer suspicions among rank-and-file workers that the claimed financial difficulties are simply the result of judicious accounting choices.

A closer look at unusual income items provides further evidence that managers systematically depressed reported earnings during union negotia- tions. For our sample, unusual items often include one-time special charges that reflect the real restructuring decisions made by sample managers during the 1980-1988 period. For example, a major capacity reduction achieved through plant closures requires that, at some point, substantial earnings charges be taken. Under current accounting rules, those charges can be taken in anticipation of, contemporaneous with, or after the economic event that triggers the earnings charge (the actual closing of plant doors), when man- agers expect the closing is permanent (a closed plant will not reopen).‘4

14See Strong and Meyer (1987), Elliott and Shaw (1988), ‘Accountants Debate Tightening Rules for ‘Big Bath’ Writeoffs by Companies’, WSJ, February 11, 1986, ‘The Half a Hit Gambit’, Forbes, December 31, 1984, ‘Rumplestilzchen Accounting’, Forbes, February 24, 1986, and ‘Big Bath? Or a Little One?‘, Forbes, October 6, 1986. Concern about the scope of managerial discretion over the timing and magnitude of noncash writeoffs has recently led the Financial Accounting Standards Board to propose new accounting standards for asset impairments.

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 19

Even though the restructuring decision requires an eventual earnings charge, managers have incentives and opportunities to accelerate (or defer) the charge into negotiation periods, thereby lowering the firm’s reported income and strengthening their bargaining position with unionized labor, both be- cause of the announced earnings charge and the permanence of the associ- ated layoffs.

To illustrate the degree of managerial discretion with respect to the timing of restructuring charges, consider those taken to 1982 earnings by Bethlehem Steel. Three days before the 1982 fiscal year end, the firm announced a special charge that ultimately totaled $1.05 billion, and that contributed to a 1982 net loss of $1.5 billion. l5 Of the total charge, $700 million was for the expected present value of termination benefits engendered by a permanent closing of facilities. Although the entire present value of these costs was charged to 1982 earnings, the primary cash flow impact will occur as benefits are paid in future periods. Another $160 million was taken for the writedown of productive facilities, effectively accelerating future years’ depreciation charges into the current period. An additional $190 million was provided for ‘other’ expected costs (primarily for anticipated ,future losses before shut- down).

Bethlehem management blamed continuing losses at the affected plants on ‘noncompetitive’ wages and benefits and on competition from a ‘continuing high level of imports’. The announcement of the proposed closings came on December 28, 1982, two months before a union agreement was reached (on March 2, 1983). The primary facility affected was the Lackawanna plant, which Bethlehem announced that it would close by the end of 1983 as part of the restructuring plan. Given the distant date of the expected closing, and the late date in the 1982 fiscal year on which the restructuring was announced, it seems reasonable to believe that Bethlehem management accelerated an- nouncement of the closings to take the $1.05 billion charge against 1982 earnings. Appendix B, which documents layoffs and plant closings, describes a number of cases in which the timing of these events differs from that of the related earnings charges.

5. Concessions by managerial and salaried personnel

We find pervasive evidence that sample firms’ requests for union concessions are accompanied by sacrifices by top management and white-collar workers. Table 5 reports regressions of changes in CEO compensation (annual salary plus bonus) on changes in company performance (annual operating cash flows), and a dummy variable that equals one in union negotiation years and zero otherwise. As expected, greater cash flow is associated with higher CEO compensation for all models. More importantly, the union dummy is uniformly negative and significant in all specifications, with t-statistics ranging from -4.55 to -4.93. We also find significantly negative values (with t-statistics from -2.48 to -3.56) for the union dummy under an error components analysis which adjusts for potential cross-sectional and time series dependence in the residuals. The significance of the union dummy is similarly robust to alternative specifica- tions in which (i) CEO compensation is replaced by that for the firm’s five highest-paid executives, and (ii) cash flow is replaced by alternative perfor- mance measures based on earnings or stock returns (details not reported here).” Thus, controlling for company performance, managerial compensa-

This inference is strongly supported by the data in appendix C, which summarizes sacrifices by managerial and salaried personnel, as reported in the WSJ. The high incidence of such sacrifices is most evident for 1982, the year in which all seven sample firms simultaneously sought wage concessions from the USW. Appendix C indicates that, in that year, six of the seven major steel producers (all except LTV) made public announcements that were carried by the WSJ of managerial and white-collar pay cuts, wage freezes, and/or benefit reductions. Overall, the WSJ articles (for 1982 and other years) indicate that large numbers of nonunion workers took pay cuts during union negotiations. Bethlehem Steel announced salary reductions for 250 high level managers (June 1982), compensation cuts for 22,000 salaried workers (July 1982), benefit reductions for all salaried employees (August 1982), and further pay cuts for 14,000 nonunion personnel (January 1983). U.S. Steel announced

wage cuts for 27,000 management and salaried personnel (June 1982), fol- lowed by further wage reductions seven months later. All of these announcements were made during union negotiations (June 1982 to March 1983). (Announcements similar in both content and timing were made by Armco, Inland, Republic, and National Steel.?

A reading of appendix C suggests that, in percentage terms, financial sacrifices by top management commonly exceed - or at least are portrayed by the firm as exceeding - those required of the firm’s other employees. And Bethlehem Steel’s CEO was apparently forced to retire early in part because his salary increases engendered strong resentment among both blue- and white-collar workers. who had themselves suffered multiple wage cuts (May 1986).

Although these reports indicate continued worker resentment of manage- rial pay, the general pattern in appendix C is one of significant compensation sacrifices by top management during union negotiations. CEO either received no bonus or the bonus was not separately disclosed.” This fact suggests that proxy disclosures are designed to reveal personal costs incurred by the CEO (by reporting that no bonus payments were made), or to diminish the likelihood of adverse publicity over CEO compensation (by not reporting bonus amounts if paid).

We find little evidence that the managerial compensation decline reported in table 6 was caused by accounting-based bonus formulas (coupled with lower reported earnings). ** While incomplete proxy disclosures make it difficult to draw strong conclusions on this issue, we did find three cases in which the bonus lost by a CEO in a union negotiation year was larger in absolute value than the decline in salary plus bonus. In one of these cases, however, the firm had a positive bonus pool which the board of directors chose not to distribute currently. In the remaining two cases, proxy disclo- sures suggest that the firm’s bonus plan gave the board the discretion to specify a positive bonus pool, but the board chose not to pay bonuses. Thus, even in these cases, discretionary board actions rather than explicit bonus plan formulas are apparently responsible for the observed decline in total salary plus bonus.

Finally, although compensation reductions were clearly substantial for (the relatively few) top managers, their dollar magnitude is obviously small rela- tive to the total dollar losses of the many thousands of union and white-collar workers who lost their jobs or experienced wage and benefit reductions. Clearly, these executive compensation reductions will not directly generate material improvements in corporate cash flow. Their indirect effects may be substantial, however, since they apparently serve to show workers that individual executives believe sufficiently in their plans to deal with the firm’s financial troubles that they too are willing to bear personal financial sacri- fices.23 In this view, ma na g erial pay cuts are not important for the dollars they save per se, but rather because they represent symbolic sacrifices that encourage all stakeholders to participate in the concessions needed to salvage the firm.

21For example, U.S. Steel’s proxy statements report that the CEO’s bonus fell from a substantial $290,000 in 1981 to zero in the union negotiation year of 1982. The firm’s proxy statements do not disclose the CEO’s bonus for 1986 (also a negotiation year), even though bonuses were disclosed in all other years and large bonuses were paid in the two prior and two subsequent years.

220ur earlier analysis suggests that the firm’s reported income is at least partly under management control, so that bonus-plan-induced cuts in managerial pay are not appropriately viewed as exogenous to managers. Rather, our findings suggest that special earnings charges and foregone bonuses are elements of a strategy chosen by managers to portray the firm as in serious trouble.

231t is possible that managerial pay was cut for other reasons as well. For example, the board of directors may have judged business conditions as sufficiently bad to require sacrifices at all levels of the organization. Another (not mutually exclusive) possibility is that executive pay cuts reflect the board’s assessment that managerial performance was especially poor.

6. Concessions by shareholders

Dividend reductions serve two complementary functions in negotiating labor concessions. Because managers are reluctant to cut dividends and risk antagonizing shareholders, a dividend reduction helps management make a credible case to the union that the firm is indeed experiencing serious financial problems. Second, members of the union rank-and-file are likely to interpret dividend cuts as concessions by shareholders. Finance theory, of course, treats the total stock market return (dividend plus equity value change) as the complete measure of shareholders’ compensation in a given period. However, the dividend component of shareholders’ total return is more likely to be viewed by the rank-and-file as shareholder ‘wage’ payments analogous to cash wages that workers receive from the firm.24

Table 8 reports the timing of dividend reductions announced during the 1980-1988 period by sample firms and the two-day stock returns associated with each announcement. The table indicates that all seven firms reduced dividends during their financial difficulties, and that all except U.S. Steel eventually omitted dividends altogether. (Although Republic Steel did not omit dividends as an independent firm, LTV did so shortly after it acquired Republic.) The high incidence of dividend omissions is notable because (i) the median firm had paid dividends for 46 continuous years,*” and (ii> managers of firms with long dividend histories appear especially reluctant to break a string of continuous dividend payments [DeAngelo and DeAngelo (1990)].

Ten of the 21 dividend reductions reported in table 8 occurred in 1982, the year in which union negotiations were opened early (in June) to accommo-

date steel firms’ request for labor concessions.26 Two firms (Bethlehem Steel and Armco) announced additional dividend reductions in January 1983, just before the USW agreed to wage concessions in March. In all, 12 of the 21 dividend reduction announcements reported in table 8 came in the period immediately preceding the USW’s initial concessionary wage agreement. Moreover, all seven sample firms announced dividend reductions during these particular union negotiations. These dividend reductions ranged from a cut of 50% (by U.S. Steel, LTV, Republic, and Inland Steel) to a cut of 87.5% (by National Steel) during the negotiation period (June 1982 to March 1983).

241n contrast, equity value changes represent the judgments of stock market traders and involve no direct resource distributions. Our focus on dividend reductions is conservative insofar as shareholders also experienced significant equity value declines (see below).

25Sample firms had paid dividends for a range of two (for LTV) to 58 (for National Steel) continuous years at the time they omitted dividends.

260f these ten dividend reductions, eight were announced after the negotiations opened in June. The other two (by Republic and Inland Steel) came about one month earlier.

As expected, sample firms’ dividend reduction announcements are associ- ated with negative stock returns. An interesting new finding is that the average stock return of -4.13% for dividend reduction announcements during union negotiations is materially less negative than the average - 7.89% return for reductions announced in nonnegotiation periods. These mean returns differ significantly at the 0.048 level under a one-tailed t-test. The median returns of - 3.26% and - 6.78% (for negotiation and nonnegotiation

Page 27

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuting of the steel industry 29

periods, respectively) differ significantly at the 0.049 level under a one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test.

The difference in average share price reactions may reflect the fact that, because steel firms’ troubles were well known in negotiation years, stock market traders could better predict dividend reductions, hence capitalize them prior to public announcement. Another possible explanation is that dividend omissions (which for our sample came during nonnegotiation peri- ods) have more negative share price consequences than do substantial cuts to a still-positive level. 27 Yet another possibility is that traders interpret divi- dend cuts during union negotiations as entailing less ‘bad news’ because in part they represent negotiating tactics designed to obtain givebacks from labor; the positive cash flows expected from these concessions partially offset the bad news usually signaled by a dividend cut.

Analysis of WSJ reports indicates that managements’ announcements of dividend reductions sometimes occur simultaneously with, or are linked explicitly to, sacrifices by unionized labor, white-collar workers, and top executives. More commonly, however, management explains the decision to reduce dividends as a cash conservation measure that was prudent and necessary in light of the firm’s financial difficulties. This fact probably reflects the reality that management is ultimately the shareholders’ agent, and must therefore be careful not to anger that constituency by appearing to retain cash that will in effect subsidize unionized labor.28 It may also help explain why managers’ case for union concessions is typically based on the firm’s general financial difficulties (which is buttressed by their willingness to risk further shareholder dissatisfaction by cutting the dividend). Although dividends were reduced substantially in percentage terms, the cash conserved through dividend reductions pales in comparison with the labor cost savings achieved through layoffs and wage cuts. The seven firms paid $463 million in common stock dividends in 1981 which, after numerous dividend reductions in 1982, declined to $201 million in 1983. Although certainly not negligible, this $262 million dividend decline is modest in relation to sample firms’ reduction in aggregate annual labor costs, which total in the billions of dollars. 29 These facts indicate that cash conserved via dividend reductions, like that from managerial pay cuts, was at best a

Rather, the importance of these reductions seems to lie in their indirect cash consequences - they foster a general cooperative spirit that all stakeholders are making material sacrifices, which encourages organized labor to make (in the aggregate, much larger) conces- sions of their own.

7. Summary and conclusions

This paper studies the effect of union negotiations on the corporate policies of the seven major domestic steel producers during the 1980s a period in which strong competitive pressures to reduce capacity led managers to negotiate major concessions from unionized labor. The resultant restruc- turing of these firms generated strikingly large reductions in productive capacity, wage bills, and total employment. Over the period 1980-1988, the seven sample firms reduced productive capacity by 38.2%. Their annual aggregate wage bill declined by 46.6% from about $16.1 billion in 1980 to around $8.6 billion in 1988, a decline achieved largely through radical employment reductions. In total, sample firms reduced employment by al- most two-thirds of their work force, for a loss of about 300,000 jobs over the decade.

Managers of domestic steel firms used a variety of approaches to help convince organized labor that their companies were in serious trouble, and therefore required major concessions. From the perspective of rank-and-file workers, the most convincing indication of serious trouble was probably the large-scale layoffs we document. We also find evidence that managers used reported losses and financial sacrifices by other (nonunion) stakeholders to support their case for labor concessions. Net income is materially lower during union negotiations than in other periods, when we control for cash flow performance. And although sample firms in the aggregate had positive cash flows in every year from 1980 to 1988, they reported losses in each of the years 1982-1986 and again in 1988. Importantly, the losses reported in union negotiation years are to a large degree driven by special earnings charges that reflect managers’ real restructuring decisions, but whose timing is discre- tionary across negotiation and nonnegotiation years. Controlling for company performance, salary plus bonus payments to CEOs (and to the five highest-paid executives) are significantly lower during union negotiations than for the same firms in other years. CEOs experienced an average 18.1% decline in salary plus bonus in union negotiation years, which contrasts markedly with their average increase of 19.5% in nonnegotia- tion years. For the five highest-paid executives, salary plus bonus declined an average 15.4% in union negotiation years, which compares with an average 16.0% increase in other years. Although managerial pay cuts are large in percentage terms (relative to the pay reductions of union and nonunion workers), their absolute magnitude is in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. The pervasive reductions in cash dividends we observe aggregate to the hundreds of millions. Both pale when compared with the billions of dollars in annual labor cost savings achieved through layoffs and wage reductions.

Page 29

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 31

workers), their absolute magnitude is in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. The pervasive reductions in cash dividends we observe aggregate to the hundreds of millions. Both pale when compared with the billions of dollars in annual labor cost savings achieved through layoffs and wage reductions.

Reductions in the compensation paid top management - although small in relation to sample firms’ total labor cost savings - apparently serve as sym- bolic actions that help foster a general attitude that financial sacrifices are required by all stakeholders. Consistent with this view, white-collar pay cuts and reductions in cash dividends are substantial on a percentage basis, pervasive, and clustered during union negotiations. Analysis of top manage- ment’s public statements indicates they cited low (and diminished) earnings, dividend cuts and omissions, white-collar pay cuts and layoffs, and reductions in their own compensation to portray the firm as in serious financial difficulty, hence in need of substantial concessions from unionized labor. Overall, then, our evidence suggests that the corporate policies of domestic steel firms requesting labor concessions during the 1980s were determined by strategic contracting considerations as well as by the firm’s technological capabilities, product market pressures, etc.

Appendix A

Chronology of union negotiations for the U.S. steel industry, 1980-1988

This chronology was developed from information in Standard & Poor’s Industry Surveys and the Wall Street Journal. Each entry contains a brief description of the relevant union activity during a given month, sometimes taken verbatim from the WSJ article.

February 1980: The United Steel Workers (USW) open contract negotiations with the steel industry. April 1980: Contract negotiations are settled, with wage and benefit hikes that are estimated to increase labor costs by 37% over the next three years.

July 1981: Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel is forced out of the Basic Industry Bargaining Group after negotiating a separate labor contract with the USW.

June 1982: USW local presidents authorize bargainers to begin informal talks with the industry even though the current labor contract is not set to expire until August 1, 1983. July 1982: Union negotiations break down. November 1982: Labor and management reach a tentative agreement, but their proposal fails to win the approval of local union presidents, raising the possibility of an industry-wide strike. December 1982: Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel negotiates a 43-month labor contract at wage reductions of $3.65 per hour (over and above the $1.60 per hour reduction the firm had negotiated in 1981) in exchange for a promise to invest the labor cost savings in steel operations, 50% sharing of pretax profits after debt service charges and dividend payments, and the issuance of preferred stock to an employee trust fund.

Page 30

32 H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry

February 1983: Union negotiations reopen. March 1983: The seven major steel firms reach agreement with the USW. The agreement reduces labor costs by $1.25 per hour in wages, eliminates certain benefits, and provides for changes in the work rules. Concessions are to be restored during the 41-month life of the contract. December 1983: U.S. Steel requests further contract concessions at live plants it is considering closing, even though multi-employer negotiations concluded earlier in the year. The USW denies the request, saying that U.S. Steel is unfairly attempting to engender competition among local workers. In response, U.S. Steel closes a number of plants and reduces other operations for a total capacity reduction of 20%, taking a $1.2 billion writeoff and reducing employment by 15,400. Of the five plants at which concessions were denied, three were closed and another had its capacity reduced substantially.

August 1984: The steelmakers’ bargaining group begins to collapse, following National Steel’s announcement that it will bargain alone when the current contract expires in two years.

April 1985: Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel files for bankruptcy. May 1985: The steel industry bargaining group collapses after a 30-year history. LTV an- nounces its intent to seek wage and benefit concessions from the USW. September 1985: LTV suspends dividends on four issues of preferred stock. October 1985: Bethlehem omits its dividend for the first time in 46 years and says it will seek to

restructure its agreement with the USW ‘well before’ the current contract expires next July 31

January 1986: LTV and Bethlehem begin separate negotiations with the USW on the contract set to expire August 1, 1986. February 1986: Armco, National, and Inland set late March target dates to negotiate new labor contracts. The USW defers scheduled wage increases for LTV, but not for Bethlehem and National. March 1986: LTV reaches a tentative agreement with the USW. Armco, National, and Bethlehem, discouraged over the terms of LTV’s labor pact and its uncertain ratification, abandon talks. Their concern is that, by negotiating first with the weakest steel producer, the USW has gained concessions that it can then impose on other steelmakers. Inland will keep bargaining. April 1986: Inland and the USW break off talks after failing to reach an agreement by the target deadline. The USW approves the contract with LTV, which provides for a $3.15 per hour reduction in labor costs with a payback schedule over time. May 1986: Bethlehem reaches a tentative accord with the union that will reduce labor costs by $1.97 per hour for one year. June 1986: U.S. Steel, the last of the major steel firms to negotiate with the USW, opens

bargaining talks. The USW approves the Bethlehem agreement. Inland Steel signs a tentative three-year pact that freezes wages, cuts benefits, and gives workers profit sharing. Armco extends the August 1 contract expiration date for three months. July 1986: LTV files for bankruptcy protection, and seeks additional concessions from the USW. The USW strikes one of the firm’s plants for a week to protest cancellation of retirees’ health and life insurance benefits until LTV reinstates them for six months. Bethlehem omits the dividend on two issues of preferred stock, citing the LTV bankruptcy filing. The Inland agreement receives final approval. U.S. Steel negotiations break down. August 1986: The USW strikes U.S. Steel. September 1986: Armco threatens to file for bankruptcy as local steelworkers strike the firm’s main plant in Middletown, Ohio. The company backs off its demands for wage concessions to settle the strike after five days with a new contract that provides only a wage and benefit freeze. Bankrupt LTV seeks to renegotiate its most recent pact with the union. October 1986: U.S. Steel resumes bargaining with the USW, as does Ammo. November 1986: Armco reaches agreement on a new labor contract that will vary from mill to mill. U.S. Steel breaks off contract talks.

January 1987: U.S. Steel reopens union negotiations, and the strike ends. February 1987: The union ratifies a four-year contract with U.S. Steel that provides for wage reductions and profit sharing. April 1987: The USW agrees to negotiate a new labor agreement with LTV by May 1, terms to be retroactive to February 1. May 2987: The USW rejects a new pact with LTV, citing provisions that would eliminate jobs

and management’s failure to sacrifice as much as steelworkers have. June 1987: LTV and the USW resume talks, and reach tentative agreement. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation threatens to return LTV’s pension obligations to the com- pany because the labor agreement restores certain supplemental pension benefits to the steelworkers, while the government continues to bear the bulk of LTV’s pension obligations, August 1987: The USW ratifies the new contract with LTV despite the PBGC’s continued legal

Appendix C

Wage and benefit reductions for top management and other salaried personnel in the U.S. steel industry, 1980-1988

This chronology was developed from information in the Wall Street Journal. Each entry contains a brief description of the relevant WSJ article, often taken verbatim from the article.

Armco Inc.

4/26/82

l/26/82

4/25/83

At the annual meeting, CEO Holiday says financial results this year probably will result in a sharp reduction or elimination of executive bonuses for 1982, and total executive compensation will be cut by 30% to 35%.

The company freezes merit raises and eliminates most bonuses for salaried employ- ees, cutting their total compensation by 15% to 30%.

At the annual meeting, CEO Holiday, apparently anticipating a hostile stockholder reaction to the latest dividend cut (the third in less than a year), tells stockholders that executive compensation for 1982 was down 44% from 1981 levels. He also says the company has suspended all contributions to the employee savings plan for all nonunion, salaried employees, and will try to negotiate a similar arrangement with employees represented by local unions.

Bethlehem Steel Corp.

6/16/82 The firm will reduce salaries of 250 high-level managers by 5% (10% for those who are both officers and directors) beginning July 1. The company also said that it probably won’t pay any bonuses this year. The reduction in total managerial compensation will be about 28% for top executives and 14% for other officers. The firm cites severe economic and competitive conditions, but some analysts see the move as a prelude to a dividend cut and as posturing before the steel industry’s labor talks start.

l/7/82 The firm announces reductions in its compensation program for 22,000 salaried workers, including 10% cuts in nonofficer directors’ fees.

8/10/82 The firm will change its compensation and benefits program for all salaried employ- ees, reducing paid time off, pension, savings, and medical benefits, and instituting an all-merit compensation program.

l/21/83 The firm will again cut the pay of more than 14,000 salaried and nonunion employees, this time by 2.5% to 8%. This action follows a similar move earlier in the week by U.S. Steel, and comes as the industry is entering a third round of bargaining with the USW.

9/30/85 The firm will further reduce wages and benefits for 10,000 salaried workers. The cuts include a 10% salary reduction for upper management, a 5% reduction in the salaries of all other salaried employees, and the elimination of the dental plan. The chairman indicates that similar contributions by hourly employees are needed to help return the firm to profitability and to help provide employment security for as many people as possible.

12/18/85 The firm scales back retirement benefits for 10,000 salaried nonunion employees. The chairman indicates that hourly workers will be expected to make similar concessions in the upcoming union negotiations (opened on l/22/86).

Page 39

H. DeAngelo and L. DeAngelo, Restructuring of the steel industry 41

5/21/86 Article reports white- and blue-collar workers’ resentment of CEO Trautlein who, along with other top managers, received a generous salary increase and golden parachute for 1985. White-collar workers have received pay cuts in three of the last four years, and the disclosure of their anger at management apparently contributed to last month’s breakdown in union negotiations. Mr. Trautlein announced his retirement (at age 59) last month.

Inland Steel Company

4/29/82 At the annual meeting, the firm announces that it is reducing the pay of about 400 executives and halving the dividend on common stock. It is also freezing the wages of many office employees, and will seek early retirement from others.

12/16/82

l/31 /83

The firm is granting smaller bonuses to salaried employees this year, but the USW is angry nonetheless because bonuses will not be eliminated. A company spokesperson justifies the action by noting that salaried workers didn’t receive merit increases this year, were denied a cost-of-living adjustment, and had medical benefits reduced. A union spokesperson says the bonuses are ‘going to make us take a long, hard look at the company’s contract proposals next year (the current contract expires July 31). If they have such a severe cash flow problem, how can they afford to give bonuses to salaried personnel?’

The firm permanently discontinues cost-of-living adjustments and eliminates two paid holidays for 5,600 salaried workers.

LTV Corporation

Article notes that LTV loaned its CEO an interest-free $1 million so he could exercise expiring stock options. The USW is infuriated, given that the loan was made in a year in which LTV had a record $378.2 million loss and that the firm has labeled recent layoffs ‘temporary’ to avoid having to pay severance benefits to union workers. The amount of the loan would have been sufficient to prevent the loss of more than 600 jobs, according to a union spokesperson.

The firm’s troubled steel unit will cut the pay of 8,000 salaried employees, effective September 1. It will also reduce a number of benefits, including vacation days and overtime. One industry source says that LTV has also drawn up a shopping list of concessions it hopes to obtain from unionized workers (union negotiations are expected to begin in December).

Chairman Hay promises further cuts in pay, benefits, and employees at corporate headquarters, and says that he himself has volunteered for a 25% pay cut.

LTV files for bankruptcy protection, and says it will seek further labor cost reductions from employees.

WSJ article reveals that the firm paid its top executives almost $1 million in performance-related compensation in 1986, the year it filed for bankruptcy protec- tion and negotiated labor givebacks. One month later, the union rejected the latest labor agreement, in part because it believes managers haven’t shouldered as much financial sacrifice as the firm’s 23,000 steelworkers.

8/26/82 The firm will cut salaries 7% to 10% for 5,800 employees. Officers’ pay cuts will be lo%, while those for supervisory and other salaried workers will be 7%. Manage- ment incentive plans, savings and investment plans, and some paid holidays were previously cut, reducing compensation of management personnel by an average of 18%.

National Steel Corp.

8/21/80

3/16/82

10/13/82

3/2/83

3/21/83

The firm cuts the dividend, noting that revenues are inadequate for the current adverse conditions, despite the firm’s cost-cutting actions, which include a reduction in all officers’ salaries. National has been especially hard hit because its product mix is tilted heavily toward flat-rolled steel for the automobile industry, which is experiencing a strong downturn.

The firm, expecting a first-quarter loss, is freezing the pay of its 7,000 salaried workers and cutting the pay of senior management by 10% to 25%. It also is discontinuing cost-of-living adjustments for salaried personnel, reducing contribu- tions to the employee stock investment plan, and eliminating some vacation benefits.

The firm will temporarily reduce base salaries by 10% for 6,000 nonunion, salaried employees, and will reinstate them ‘as soon as business conditions permit’. The cuts apply to personnel in all operating units and at company headquarters, but not to those at the firm’s financial services subsidiary.

The USW ratifies the new labor contract for the steel industry.

The firm cancels the previously-announced 10% salary reduction for nonunion personnel, but will still cut fringe benefits. A company spokesperson says: ‘The changes are being made to bring the levels of sacrifice closer to those being made by our hourly workers, and they also expand and make permanent labor cost savings for the present and long term.’

U.S. Steel Corporation

5/20/80 The firm institutes a freeze on managerial (at all ranks) pay less than a month after the completion of union negotiations that granted double-digit wage increases to steelworkers.

3/12/81 The firm seeks shareholder approval to eliminate the effect of such unusual events as plant closings and asset sales on top management’s incentive compensation.

6/22/82 The firm will cut compensation benefits of about 27,000 management and salaried employees. Wages are to be cut by at least 5%, with managerial personnel suffering cuts of up to 30% because their incentive compensation will be suspended for 1982. (Incentive pay totaled $3.4 million in 1981.) This announcement is seen as tactical posturing by the steel industry, which is preparing to ask the USW for wage and benefit concessions.

l/17/83 The firm says it expects to report a ‘staggering’ fourth-quarter loss and will cut the pay of 28,000 management, salaried, and nonunion hourly workers by 5%. The timing of the second nonunion pay cut in seven months is seen as a move to strengthen the industry’s position when it again asks the USW next month for steep pay and benefit concessions. Chairman Roderick alleges that only the USW has refused to contribute to the sacrifices made by everyone else in the steel family to ensure the survival of the company.

USX plans to extend (previously announced: date unknown) pay cuts to its Marathon Oil and Texas Oil & Gas units. The cuts, said to be 12% for top officials and 6% for lower-level managers, follow similar cuts for its corporate staff and steelmaking and diversified business units.

USX discloses that top management took pay cuts of about 25% in 1986 as a result of a series of austerity measures adopted when the USW struck the firm in August. However, they also received golden parachutes that would pay as much as three times their salaries plus incentive bonuses if they lost their jobs following a hostile takeover.
